subsection: 8. The impact of the Troubles on the economy and society

notes.b: The Troubles (the conflict in Northern Ireland that began in 1969 and continued into the 1990s and beyond) caused thousands of deaths and injuries. Here the focus is the human cost and where it fell, not the causes or events.
points: Between 1969 and 1993 the Troubles caused about 3,000 deaths. The total for the whole conflict to about 2001 is about 3,500 or more, and figures vary by source, so always say "about".
1972 was the deadliest year of the Troubles, with nearly 500 deaths.
About half of the dead were civilians. Members of the security forces (the army and police), republican paramilitaries and loyalist paramilitaries also died in large numbers.
Tens of thousands of people were injured, and the harm was psychological as well as physical, because survivors and the bereaved lived with trauma.

The violence was concentrated in Belfast, especially north and west Belfast, in Derry and in the border counties. Working-class districts such as Ardoyne, the Falls and the Shankill in Belfast, and the Bogside in Derry, suffered most.
Most deaths took place in Northern Ireland, though bombings in Britain and the Republic also caused deaths, including the Dublin and Monaghan bombings of 1974 in the Republic.
notes.tip: Give the figures as plain, dated facts: about 3,000 deaths 1969-93, about half civilians, tens of thousands injured. Never quote a precise number for deaths or injuries beyond these.

notes.b: Violence made Northern Ireland look like a risky place to do business or take a holiday. Investment and tourism fell, and the cost of insurance and security rose for businesses across the province.
points: Foreign investors were reluctant to open or expand factories in Northern Ireland because of the risk of bombing, disruption and bad publicity, so jobs that might have replaced declining industries never arrived.
Tourism fell sharply because visitors avoided the province. This hurt hotels, shops and the wider local economy that depended on visitors' spending.
Bomb attacks damaged city-centre trade. From 1972 a security zone with barriers and gates surrounded central Belfast, popularly called the ring of steel, and the checks discouraged shoppers.

Businesses faced high insurance premiums to cover bomb damage and had to spend on security. Some companies closed or moved their operations to Britain or the Republic, which put further pressure on local jobs.
Security measures, such as checkpoints and searches, increased the time and cost of moving goods and people.
The government paid compensation for criminal damage under official schemes, which added to public spending.
notes.tip: A strong answer gives at least two economic examples with their reason, such as investors put off by bombing and high insurance costs. Do not treat the economy as a single list item.

notes.h: Decline of manufacturing and growth of public-sector employment
notes.b: Before 1969 the economy depended heavily on shipbuilding, linen and engineering, and in the 1960s new industries, including man-made fibres, were promoted to modernise it. Manufacturing then kept shrinking while public-sector and security jobs grew, so the province became more dependent on the British state.
points: Manufacturing employment continued to decline, so many workers lost their jobs, with shipbuilding, linen, engineering and man-made fibres all shedding jobs through the 1970s and 1980s.
This decline began before 1969 and had international causes, including wider recession, so the Troubles worsened it rather than caused it alone.
Harland and Wolff, the Belfast shipyard, was taken into public ownership in 1975 because the government wished to protect jobs.
Public-sector employment (jobs paid for by government, such as health, education and local administration) grew as a share of the workforce.

The security sector also provided many jobs: the Ulster Defence Regiment (formed 1970 and merged into the Royal Irish Regiment in 1992), the RUC (the police), the prison service, the army and private security.
British subvention, the public money transferred from the Treasury (the British finance ministry) to cover the gap, kept public services and living standards above what local output could pay for.

Because the public sector was so large, Northern Ireland's economy was exposed to any change in British government spending. Subvention is not the same as British security spending, though the two are related.
notes.tip: Link the points: the Troubles added security jobs and subvention, which made the economy dependent on Britain. Do not say the decline of manufacturing was caused only by the Troubles.

notes.b: The De Lorean factory at Dunmurry, south-west Belfast, was a government-backed attempt to bring in investment and jobs. It collapsed in 1982 and cost the taxpayer heavily.
points: The DeLorean Motor Company built a factory at Dunmurry to make a stainless-steel sports car. Production began in 1981, funded by British government grants and loans of tens of millions of pounds.

The factory was intended to create about 2,000 jobs in an area of high unemployment. The site lay between Catholic and Protestant housing estates, in the hope of drawing both communities into work, though the workforce was never as mixed as hoped.
The car sold poorly, so the company went into receivership (was taken over by an administrator because it could not pay its debts) in February 1982.
John De Lorean, the man behind the company, was arrested in the USA in October 1982 on a drug-trafficking charge and was acquitted in August 1984. His case is separate from the company's failure.
The collapse left the British government with heavy losses. It showed both the government's willingness to subsidise investment and the difficulty of attracting investors to Northern Ireland.
notes.tip: Do not tell it as a story. Say what it shows: government willingness to subsidise investment, its failure, and the difficulty of attracting investors.

notes.b: Unemployment stayed well above the UK average, and it fell unequally: Catholics were out of work far more often than Protestants. Governments responded with fair employment law, and campaigners abroad with the MacBride Principles.
points: Unemployment in Northern Ireland was above the UK average through the 1970s and 1980s.

Catholic unemployment was consistently higher than Protestant unemployment, roughly twice as high. Causes include discrimination, location in the west of the province, and the sectors where Catholics worked.

The Fair Employment (Northern Ireland) Act 1976 set up a Fair Employment Agency to investigate discrimination in employment. It could not compel employers to monitor their workforces, so its power was limited.
The Fair Employment (Northern Ireland) Act 1989 replaced the Agency with a Fair Employment Commission, required employers to monitor their workforce by religion, and brought stronger enforcement.
The MacBride Principles of 1984, named after Sean MacBride, were a code of fair employment for US firms operating in Northern Ireland, promoted by Irish-American campaigners.
West Belfast and Derry suffered the highest deprivation (poor housing, income and opportunity), with families who had lost jobs and had few alternative sources of income.
Historians link unemployed young men, especially young Catholic men in the 1980s, to recruitment to paramilitaries. This is a link they raise, not a proven single cause.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the dated laws: the 1976 Act investigated and advised, while the 1989 Act required monitoring and had stronger powers. Name the date and what each did.

notes.h: Housing: the Housing Executive, population movement and peace walls
notes.b: Catholic complaints about housing allocation had been central to the civil rights movement before 1969. The Housing Executive was set up to answer them, but violence pushed communities apart faster than policy could bring them together.
points: The Northern Ireland Housing Executive was established in 1971 to take over public housing from the local councils and the Northern Ireland Housing Trust.
It allocated houses by a points system based on need, so that religion no longer decided who got a house, to end the discrimination that the civil rights movement had criticised.

Intimidation (threats and violence meant to force people out) drove families from mixed areas into areas where their own community was the majority. Tens of thousands of people moved home in Belfast between 1969 and 1973.

Peace walls (also called peace lines) are barriers between Protestant and Catholic streets. They were first built in Belfast in 1969, grew in number in the 1970s and 1980s, and were later built in Derry and elsewhere.
Peace walls were built to protect people, but they also reinforced the segregation that intimidation had created.
Segregation made communities more distinct, so it made it harder for people from different backgrounds to meet.
Segregation cut across the Executive's allocation policy in practice, because families moved from mixed areas into segregated estates.
notes.tip: Show the chain of cause and effect: intimidation caused segregation, which fed the demand for peace walls. Remember the first peace walls were in Belfast, not Derry.

notes.b: Schools remained largely divided by religion throughout the Troubles. A small, parent-led integrated movement began in the 1970s, and the state gave it legal support in 1989.
points: Most children went to either Catholic maintained schools or mainly Protestant controlled schools, so the school system mirrored the religious divisions of the province.
The Catholic Church controlled its schools and defended its right to do so, so Catholic voluntary schools kept state support, and the system stayed divided.
Teacher training was also separate: Catholic teachers trained mainly at St Mary's College and Protestants at Stranmillis College, both in Belfast.
The integrated education movement began when parents in both communities formed All Children Together in 1974 to campaign for mixed schools.
Lagan College, opened in Belfast in September 1981 with 28 pupils, was the first integrated secondary school in Northern Ireland.
The Education Reform (Northern Ireland) Order of 1989 gave statutory (legal) support to integrated schools. It placed a duty on the Department of Education to encourage and facilitate them.
Integrated schools were few by 1993 and at first depended on parents and charitable funding, so most children remained in separate schools.
notes.tip: Keep the three dates apart: All Children Together was the parents' campaign in 1974, Lagan College opened in 1981, and the Education Reform Order came in 1989. Mention that integrated schools stayed few.

notes.h: Health: trauma care and mental health
notes.b: The health service had to treat the wounded of a violent conflict, and the strain of living through it left lasting psychological harm.
points: The Royal Victoria Hospital on the Falls Road in Belfast developed world-leading expertise in treating gunshot wounds and blast injuries, and its surgeons' experience was used elsewhere.
Because the casualties were so many, hospitals and ambulance crews had to treat large numbers of injured civilians and members of the security forces, which placed heavy demands on staff.
Ambulance crews and hospital staff faced danger when responding to bomb incidents.
Mental health problems, such as stress and trauma, were widespread among people who had lived through bombings, shootings, bereavement and displacement.
Security measures and fear of attack affected access to health care, through delays and restrictions on movement.

In 1973 health and personal social services were reorganised into four Health and Social Services Boards (Eastern, Northern, Southern and Western). This was an administrative reform, not a result of the Troubles.
notes.tip: Name the Royal Victoria Hospital and what it was expert in, gunshot and blast injuries. Do not claim the Troubles caused the 1973 reorganisation.

notes.b: Beyond the headline events, the Troubles changed ordinary routines. Security measures and community division shaped how people shopped, travelled and grew up, especially in Belfast and Derry.
points: Because of the threat of bombs, security checkpoints, searches and vehicle checks were a feature of daily life in Belfast and Derry, and they changed the routines of shopping and travel.
Town centres were sealed or controlled after bombings, with security gates, so shoppers had to pass through checks to enter them.
Car bombs prompted security checks and car-park controls in city-centre shopping areas.
In divided towns and estates, some people avoided areas where the other community lived, which limited social contact.
Children grew up, for example, with soldiers and barriers around them and with memories of violence in their local areas.
notes.tip: Use everyday life for the social strand of a 100-mark essay, with at least two examples such as checkpoints, sealed town centres or avoidance of the other community's areas.

notes.b: Examiners reward a judgement on how serious the impact was. Weigh the costs against the reforms, and compare how people at the time and historians since have seen it.
points: Cost: investment, tourism and manufacturing were damaged, and the economy came to rely on public money and the security sector.
Cost: segregation in housing and schooling deepened the social divisions between the communities.
Achievement: the Housing Executive, the Fair Employment Acts and integrated schools were real reforms towards equal treatment in housing, jobs and education.
Limit: the Catholic-Protestant gap in unemployment and deprivation persisted, which means reforms were incomplete, and integrated schools were few.
Contemporary view: unionists pointed to public investment and the British subvention as proof that the state supported the province.
Contemporary view: nationalists argued that discrimination and deprivation were rooted in state policy and that the Troubles had made them worse.
Later view: historians stress that the Troubles were both a cause and a consequence of inequality, and that the costs fell on both communities, most heavily on working-class areas.
The impact was uneven: some areas, and middle-class suburbs, were largely untouched.
notes.tip: Cover both economic and social strands with at least two dated examples each, then give a judgement. Writing only about deaths, or only about the economy, scores poorly.

keyTerms.definition: The public money transferred from the British Treasury to Northern Ireland to fund services and support living standards beyond what local output could pay for.
The public body established in 1971 to take over public housing from the local councils and allocate housing.
Barriers built from 1969 onwards between Protestant and Catholic streets in Belfast to reduce violence between neighbourhoods.
Legislation and agencies introduced from 1976 to investigate and prevent discrimination in employment on religious grounds.
Schooling in which Protestant and Catholic children are taught together, promoted from the 1970s as an alternative to segregated schools.
Threats and violence used to force people to leave their homes or areas, which drove population movement and housing segregation.
Jobs in government services such as health, education, administration and security, which grew as a share of the workforce.
Lack of income, jobs, housing and services, which was most severe in the working-class areas most affected by the Troubles.
A 1984 code of fair employment practice promoted by Irish-American campaigners for US companies operating in Northern Ireland.
The first integrated secondary school in Northern Ireland, opened in Belfast in 1981.
The government-funded car factory at Dunmurry that opened in 1981 and collapsed into receivership in 1982.
